Abstract
Introduction  Public health today is challenged by a wide array of hazards that threaten humans, often resulting in 
high rates of morbidity and mortality when they strike. These events should be detected and responded to as early 
as possible to save lives and minimize their impact. The Epidemic Intelligence from Open Sources (EIOS) system 
leverages natural language processing and machine learning techniques for the early detection of public health 
events from open-source information using an all-hazards approach. In this study, we quantitatively evaluate the 
performance of the EIOS system for the early detection of outbreaks and health emergencies in the African region.
Methods  We retrospectively searched the EIOS system to determine if a signal was found on the system for each 
public health event notified to WHO by the 47 countries in the African region from 2018 to 2023. We computed 
the proportion of public health event detected by the EIOS system, its sensitivity, harmonic mean, and timeliness. 
We assessed the association between selected predictors (year of report, hazard type, subregion, source type, and 
language of source) and early detection of public health events on the EIOS system using a multivariable logistic 
regression model.
Results  We found a detection proportion of 81.0% and a sensitivity of 47.4%, with a harmonic mean of 59.8%. The 
proportion of events detected steadily increased over the years and sensitivity increased from a baseline of 44.1% in 
2018 to 47.3% in 2023. Signals for more than 80.0% of the public health events notified to WHO in 28 countries were 
detected on the EIOS system. In 22 countries, signals of at least 50% of the public health events were detected early, 
that is, before official notification from the National Authorities to WHO. The median time between detection on the 
EIOS system and notification to WHO was zero days. We found that the type of hazard (infectious and zoonotic), the 
subregion (West and Central Africa), and the type of source (medical and social media) were associated with early 
detection.

Introduction
In today’s global landscape, the challenges to public 
health are ever evolving and multifaceted. The spectrum 
of public health risks encompasses a wide array of haz­
ards, including infectious and non-infectious diseases 
[1], conflicts [2], natural disasters [3], climate change [4], 
chemical pollutants, and various environmental hazards 
[5], which continue to pose threats that transcend bor­
ders and challenge our collective resilience. These factors 
collectively contribute to significant morbidity and mor­
tality rates across the globe. The African region, where 
fragile healthcare systems [6] are among the amplify­
ing factors, remains vulnerable, often experiencing high 
impact when these public health events strike [7].
The advent of the digital age and the proliferation of 
information technology boosted the role of the Internet 
as an invaluable source of information for public health 
intelligence [8]. The ubiquity and utilization of informa­
tion technology enable online user-generated data to 
offer information and insights, particularly from sources 
like social media, thus providing timely leads on potential 
public health events, sometimes preceding official inves­
tigations and announcements from national authorities.
In 2018, the Epidemic Intelligence from Open Sources 
(EIOS) system was introduced as an innovation for pub­
lic health intelligence that amalgamates existing inter­
net-based surveillance networks, digital or web-based 
resources, and social media platforms [9], enabling the 
World Health Organization (WHO), its partners, and 
member states, to proactively detect, verify, assess, 
and communicate about potential public health threats 
through the utilization of publicly available information. 
As a web-based access-restricted system developed by 
the Joint Research Centre (JRC) of the European Com­
mission in collaboration with the WHO [10], the system 
builds on advances in artificial intelligence by leverag­
ing natural language processing and machine learning 
techniques to scrape and process thousands of pieces 
of information or articles daily from various sources on 
the web such as websites of organizations, social media, 
news aggregators, blogs, and expert groups. This Open-
Source Intelligence (OSINT) system employs text min­
ing and analytical modules to categorize these articles by 
language, topics, country, source and contextual indices 
using keywords for geolocation, entity recognition, and 
disease or event categories. It also enables deduplica­
tion by identifying and tagging articles that are at least 
99% similar in content. The outputs are displayed on a 
portal and accessible interface through which registered 
users and organizations can apply custom filters to select 
specific information for specific locations and collabo­
rate within their own space, securely sharing information 
within and across organizations.
The use of the EIOS system in the African region has 
rapidly expanded, with the onboarding of 34 countries 
and the training of over 900 users in these countries by 
the end of 2023. However, no study has been conducted 
to assess the performance of the EIOS system in the early 
detection of outbreaks and health emergencies in the 
African region despite the system’s growing utilization. 
As such, there is a pressing need for empirical evidence 
demonstrating its effectiveness for early detection. This 
evidence is crucial to persuade policymakers and public 
health practitioners of its utility and to promote funding 
for further development.
The aim of this study, therefore, is to quantitatively 
evaluate the effectiveness of the EIOS system in the early 
detection of outbreaks and health emergencies in the 
African region from open-source information compared 
to the gold standard, which is the official notification by 
national governments to WHO as per the requirements 
of the International Health Regulations (IHR 2005) [11]. 
It is anticipated that the findings from this study will not 
only establish evidence of the usefulness of the EIOS sys­
tem and discern the factors that influence its effectiveness 
but also inform the further refinement and utilization of 
this system, enhancing its contribution to the landscape 
of public health intelligence in Africa and beyond.
Methods
Study design and setting
This study employs a retrospective observational study 
design to evaluate the performance of the EIOS system 
in detecting outbreaks and health emergencies notified 
to WHO from 47 African countries1 spanning a six-year 
period, from 2018 to 2023.
Data sources, collection, and classification
The primary dataset used in this study was a list of all 
public health events notified to WHO by the countries in 
the African region from 2018 to 2023. This information

Conclusions  We conclude that the EIOS system performed well in detecting public health events in the African 
region early. However, some improvements are needed. We recommend increasing social media and local community 
radio sources on the EIOS system.

was compiled, verified, and recorded in the Public Health 
Events Dataset (PHED) by epidemiologists at the WHO 
Regional Office for Africa (AFRO). Epidemiologists at 
AFRO verify notifications through an established pro­
cess that includes cross-checking reports with the WHO 
Country Offices and the IHR Focal Point at AFRO. Upon 
obtaining permission from AFRO, we accessed the PHED 
to acquire key information relevant to the study period. 
Specifically, for each public health event, we extracted 
the name of the affected country that notified the event, 
the type of event, and the date it was officially notified to 
WHO.
We searched the EIOS system retrospectively to iden­
tify a corresponding signal for each public health event 
recorded in the primary dataset. A signal is information 
about a potential acute public health event detected from 
sources other than the official notifications from coun­
tries to WHO and is subject to verification [12]. When 
found, the date of publication on the EIOS system, the 
source type, and the original language of publication 
were extracted and appended to the primary dataset. To 
capture both early and late publications, an initial time 
filter encompassing four weeks before and after the date 
of notification of the event to WHO was created on the 
EIOS system. The selection of this time frame is based on 
findings which show that, in some instances, it can take 
nearly a month from the first available informal infor­
mation about a public health event before official decla­
ration by the government [13]. When a corresponding 
signal of an acute public health event was not found on 
the EIOS system during this initial time period, a second 
search was performed using the entire time period of the 
study. Also, to ensure that we did not miss any signal on 
the EIOS system about a particular public health event, 
we filtered by categories and mentioned geographic areas 
using keywords contained in the information about the 
public health event, such as disease or event name, signs 
and symptoms, and name of the country or subregion 
affected. The unknown category in the EIOS system was 
also selected for all searches to ensure that we did not 
miss any signals of acute public health events, even if 
the diagnosis was not known at the time of publication 
on the system. This search was also performed indepen­
dently by a second reviewer, an epidemiologist in AFRO’s 
public health intelligence team, to ensure accuracy.
Public health events notified to WHO were classified as 
detected early (DE), detected late (DL), or not detected 
(ND) based on the timing of the signal on the EIOS sys­
tem. A public health event was considered as detected 
early (DE) if a signal about the event was published on the 
EIOS system prior to the official notification of the event 
to WHO by the country. A public health event was con­
sidered as detected late (DL) if a signal about the event 
was published on the EIOS system after the event was 
officially notified to WHO. When an event was notified 
on the same date it was published on the EIOS system, 
we compare the earliest time of publication on the EIOS 
system with the time the notification report was received 
by WHO to determine if it was detected early or late by 
the EIOS system. A public health event was considered as 
not detected (ND) if no signal about the event was found 
to be published on the EIOS system. When multiple sig­
nals about the same event or a duplicate of the informa­
tion was found, the article with the earliest date and time 
of publication on the EIOS system was selected.
Inclusion and exclusion criteria
Only acute public health events notified to WHO by 
countries in the African region from 2018 to 2023 were 
included in the study. Public health events not detected 
by the EIOS system were excluded from the analysis on 
timeliness.
Performance metrics
We computed the EIOS system’s detection rate, sensitiv­
ity, and timeliness. The aggregate count of public health 
events detected early, late, and not detected were desig­
nated as DET, DLT, and NDT respectively. The propor­
tion of events detected (DR) measures the EIOS system’s 
ability to capture a signal of an acute public health event 
before or after notification to WHO within the time 
period of the study. It was calculated as DR = (DET + DLT) 
/ (DET + DLT + NDT) * 100. Sensitivity (SE) measures the 
EIOS system’s ability to capture a signal of an acute pub­
lic health event before it was officially notified to WHO 
within the time period of the study. It was calculated as 
SE = DET / (DET + DLT + NDT) * 100. To mitigate against 
the impact of outliers and provide a more balanced view 
of the EIOS system’s performance, we computed the har­
monic mean (H) between detection proportion and sen­
sitivity. It was computed as H = 2 * (DR * SE) / (DR + SE). 
Timeliness measures the duration between the date of 
the earliest publication of a signal on the EIOS system 
and the date of notification of the corresponding public 
health event to WHO.
Predictor variables
We selected the following predictors a priori to assess 
their association with early detection on the EIOS sys­
tem: year of report (2018, 2019, 2020, 2021, 2022, and 
2023); hazard type (infectious, zoonosis, disaster, oth­
ers); subregion (Central, East, Southern, and West 
Africa); types of sources (medical, non-governmental 
organizations, radio/TV, social media, web news) and 
language of source (English, French, Portuguese, and 
Others). These predictors are defined in Table  1. The 
year of report was chosen as a predictor to evaluate the 
performance of the EIOS system over time, considering

that updates or refinement in algorithms and temporal 
trends in public health threats and reporting practices 
might account for changes in performance over time. We 
used the WHO classification of public health events into 
hazard categories [14]. All public health events notified 
to WHO during the study period were classified accord­
ing to the hazard categories chosen for this study. While 
we acknowledge that zoonotic hazards are infectious in 
nature, we have set diseases in this category apart from 
other infectious diseases to emphasize their frequency, 
pandemic potential, diverse transmission pathways, eco­
nomic impact, and the need for a One Health approach 
to control them effectively. We also chose subregion as 
a predictor to enhance understanding of how the EIOS 
system performs across different geographical, epidemio­
logical, and socio-political contexts in the African region, 
given subregional disparities in surveillance capacities, 
reporting practices, and public health threats. The types 
of sources considered in this study are based on how the 
sources of articles are classified in the EIOS system. The 
languages were also chosen because they represented the 
predominant languages in which articles were published 
on the EIOS system about events in the African region.
Data analysis
We used descriptive statistics to analyze the detection 
status of public health events and performance metrics 
of the EIOS system, categorized by year of report and 
hazard type. Geospatial analysis was conducted by map­
ping the distribution of the proportion of events detected 
across countries.
For detected public health events, we cross-tabulated 
the outcome status (detected early and late) with the pre­
dictor variables and checked for associations between the 
categories using Pearson’s chi-square test. Additionally, 
we computed timeliness, expressed in median time (in 
days) for the detected public health events, disaggregated 
by the predictors.
Univariable and multivariable logistic regression analy­
ses were employed to assess the association between the 
predictors and early detection of public health events on 
the EIOS system. A backward stepwise selection process 
was used to select the final multivariable logistics regres­
sion model using the lowest Akaike information criterion 
(AIC). The results of the logistic regression models are 
presented as odds ratios (OR) for the univariable model 
and adjusted odds ratio (AOR) for the multivariable 
model, with a 95% confidence interval (CI).
All analyses were performed using R version 4.2.1 [15].

Ethics
This study utilizes publicly available information sourced 
by the EIOS system, No personally identifying informa­
tion was obtained or presented in the analysis. The study 
does not involve human subjects or experiments. We 
obtained ethical waiver and permission from AFRO to 
use the data for analyses.
Results
From 2018 to 2023, the countries in the African Region 
notified 646 public health events to WHO (Table  2). 
Of these, most (n = 430, 66.6%) were infectious disease 
outbreaks. Table  2 also shows that 306 (47.4%) public 
health events were detected early in the EIOS System, 
217 (33.6%) were detected late, and 123 (19.0%) were not 
detected. The overall proportion of events detected was 
81%, increasing from 75.7% in 2018 to 87.5% by 2023. 
Except for a slight drop in 2019, the proportion of events 
detected increased steadily. The overall sensitivity was 
47.4%, with a modest increase from 44.1% in 2018 to 
47.3% in 2023, despite annual fluctuations. The harmonic 
mean also increased from 55.7% in 2018 to 61.4% in 2023, 
with fluctuations over the years. The EIOS system met­
rics were higher for events in the disaster (man-made 
and natural) category, with a detection proportion of 
94.2%, sensitivity of 73.1%, and harmonic mean of 82.3% 
(Table 2).
Figure 1 shows that after a slight increase between 2018 
and 2019, the proportion of events not detected in the 
EIOS system consistently declined from 25.2% in 2019 to 
12.5% in 2023. Early detection was highest in 2022, with 
56.9% of all public health events in the African region 
detected early in the EIOS system. The events detected 
late increased from 31.5% in 2018 to 40.2% in 2023, also 
exhibiting fluctuations over time (Fig. 1).
There were ten countries (Botswana, Equatorial 
Guinea, Eritrea, Eswatini, Lesotho, Mauritius, Nige­
ria, Rwanda, Sao Tome and Principe, and Seychelles) in 
which all the public health events notified to WHO were 
also detected in the EIOS system (Fig. 2). An additional 
18 countries (Algeria, Angola, Benin, Central African 
Republic, Chad, Democratic Republic of the Congo, 
Ghana, Liberia, Madagascar, Malawi, Mozambique, 
Namibia, Sierra Leone, South Africa, South Sudan, Togo, 
Uganda, Zimbabwe), had detection proportion above 
80%, giving a total of 28 countries with detection propor­
tion above 80%. Figure 2 also shows 17 countries (Burkina 
Faso, Burundi, Cameroon, Cape Verde, Comoros, Congo, 
Cote d’Ivoire, Ethiopia, Gambia, Guinea, Kenya, Mali, 
Mauritania, Niger, Senegal, Tanzania, and Zambia) with 
detection proportions between 50 and 80%. Less than 
50% of the events in two countries, Guinea-Bissau and 
Gabon, were detected (Fig. 2).
In four countries (Botswana, Eritrea, Sao Tome and 
Principe, and Seychelles) all the public health events were 
detected early in the EIOS system. An additional 18 coun­
tries (Algeria, Angola, Burkina Faso, Democratic Repub­
lic of the Congo, Ghana, Madagascar, Malawi, Mauritius, 
Mozambique, Namibia, Nigeria, Rwanda, Sierra Leone, 
South Africa, South Sudan, Togo, Zambia, and Zimba­
bwe) had at least 50% of the public health events detected 
early in the EIOS system, bringing to 22 the total number 
of countries with at least 50% of the public health events 
detected early in the EIOS system before official notifica­
tion to WHO (Fig. 2).

hazard types (Table 3). We also found a statistically sig­
nificant difference in the outcomes (early and late detec­

The median time to detection was zero days (IQR − 4, 
5) (Table 4). No significant difference in median time to 
detection was observed over the years and for other pre­
dictor categories (Table 4).
Infectious and zoonotic hazards were significantly 
associated with early detection in the EIOS system com­
pared to disasters (Table 5). The odds of being detected 
earlier were 2.5 times and 3.5 times higher, respectively, 
compared to disasters. The odds of being detected 
early were also significantly higher (p < 0.05) in Central 
Africa [AOR = 2.73; 95%CI (1.44, 5.25)] and West Africa 
[AOR = 2.35; 95%CI (1.36, 4.13)] compared to Southern 
Africa. Medical sources [AOR = 1.76; 95%CI (1.18, 2.63)] 
and social media sources [AOR = 3.45; 95%CI (1.51, 8.27)] 
were significantly associated with early detection com­
pared to web news. No other stratifying variable had a 
significant association with early detection in the EIOS 
system (Table 5).
Discussion
Our study findings showed improved and balanced per­
formance of the EIOS system over the years, both in 
terms of the proportion of events detected and sensitivity. 
By providing early information to WHO compared to 
official notifications from countries for nearly half of the 
public health events that occurred in the African region, 
the EIOS system proved to be an effective public health 
intelligence tool facilitating early detection and response 
to save lives and mitigate the impact of these events in 
the African region. The increased detection rates since 
2018 were influenced by the expansion of the use of the 
EIOS system in the African region, with new sources and 
categories being added as countries were onboarded, the­
oretically enhancing the system’s ability to capture more 
signals about acute public health events in the African 
region. Consistent with our findings, Choi et al. found 
that web-based surveillance systems are intuitive, adapt­
able, and can operate in real-time [16] as a valuable tool 
for public health intelligence. This encouraging perfor­
mance is a result of how cutting-edge innovations such 
as artificial intelligence, including machine learning tech­
niques have enhanced capacities and improved the per­
formance of web-based systems in detecting outbreaks 
and other public health events [16, 17].
The varying performance of the EIOS system across the 
countries studied could be attributed to several factors, 
including but not limited to the number of online sources 
available in the system mediated by varying internet

organizations and sources, restrictions on internet access 
and online freedom, skewed internet access between 
urban and rural areas, and national bureaucracies asso­
ciated with the notification process. For example, the 
EIOS system proportion of public health events detected 
in Seychelles, Botswana, Mauritius, and South Africa 
were among the highest. These countries also have rela­
tively high mobile technology and internet penetration 
in Africa [18], with numerous news and organizational 
websites, online newspapers, and active social media 
platforms accounting for the availability of open-source 
information. On the other hand, restrictions on internet 
access and online freedom imposed by some govern­
ments [19] could impact the availability of online sources 
for public health information.
In addition to the plausible explanation of variation in 
detection proportions based on internet penetration and 
availability of online sources within countries, other fac­
tors mentioned are worth consideration. For example, all 
public health events in Eritrea, a country with a relatively 
low internet penetration, were detected early in the EIOS 
system. A thorough review showed that the EIOS system 
sourced this information from global media outlets and 
online engagements from the Eritrean diaspora popula­
tion. These global media outlets tend to be crucial sources 
of information where local sources are inadequate or 
inaccessible. Additionally, the online engagements of 
the large Eritrean diaspora population allowed the EIOS 
system to source information beyond the local sources. 
Another interesting factor to consider is that sometimes, 
depending on the nature and magnitude of the pub­
lic health event, official notifications from governments 
may encounter bureaucratic delays, allowing time for the 
EIOS system to source such information before official 
notification to the WHO. Furthermore, internet accessi­
bility may be more concentrated in urban areas in some 
countries [20, 21], thereby limiting access in rural areas, 
where some public health events have occurred.
Open-source information is valuable and reliable for 
high-impact events caused by disasters as they typi­
cally generate immediate and widespread media cover­
age [22], providing timely and detailed information for 
public health intelligence. Thus, the finding of high pro­
portion of public health events detected and sensitivity 
for disasters compared to other types of hazards is not 
unexpected. However, the EIOS system sources news 
from many expert networks and systems like ProMED 
[23], HealthMap [24], and others dedicated to provid­
ing real-time information on infectious disease threats 
and outbreaks. Furthermore, news about infectious dis­
ease outbreaks, including those of zoonotic origin, usu­
ally generates concern from public health authorities and 
heightened media interest, leading to quicker reporting 
through publicly available platforms. This could account 
for the higher proportion of infectious and zoonotic dis­
ease outbreaks being detected early and the strong asso­
ciation found between the EIOS system’s ability to detect 
infectious and zoonotic disease outbreaks earlier com­
pared to disasters.
The overall median time to detection of zero days 
indicates that, for many public health events, the detec­
tion occurred either around the time of notification or 
very early in relation to the notification, with the cen­
tral tendency of detection times clustered around the 
notification period. The public health intelligence team 
at AFRO closely monitored the EIOS system daily and 
sent verification requests to countries whenever a signal 
was detected [25]. This rigorous process and exchange 
with countries facilitated faster official notifications in 
response to verification requests from the AFRO public 
health intelligence team. These responses, usually within 
24 h of receipt by countries, likely reduced the time lag 
between detection on the EIOS system and official noti­
fication to WHO.
The study also found that the odds of detecting a public 
health event early were significantly higher in Central and 
West Africa compared to Southern Africa. Several factors 
might explain this finding. Central and West Africa expe­
rienced a higher incidence of infectious disease events, 
leading to more frequent reporting and quicker detection 
compared to Southern Africa. These regions have previ­
ous experience with large-scale epidemics like Ebola [26, 
27], which has led to heightened media sensitivity over 
the years, contributing to quicker dissemination of infor­
mation online and through other publicly available chan­
nels. People in Central and West Africa might be using 
the internet, including social media, more proactively to 
share information about outbreaks, given their experi­
ence, thus facilitating faster detection by internet-based 
systems like the EIOS system. Additionally, numerous 
NGOs involved in health service delivery, including pub­
lic health surveillance, operate in these regions. These 
organizations often report information about events 
early, sometimes before official government channels.
Social media continues to grow in importance as a 
critical source of early information about public health 
events (36). This growth is consistent with our findings 
which showed that social media and medical news were 
more closely associated with the early detection of pub­
lic health events on the EIOS system than Web news. 
Although only a small proportion of public health events 
were identified through social media, it proved to be a 
valuable source of early information. This finding sug­
gests that integrating more social media sources into 
the EIOS system could be crucial for enhancing the sys­
tem’s ability to detect public health events early. Addi­
tionally, expert systems dedicated to medical news, like

HealthMap and ProMED, have proven to be reliable early 
sources of information on the EIOS system.
The EIOS system is built to be language-agnostic, col­
lecting and processing data from various sources in mul­
tiple languages using automated translation and natural 
language processing. This technical requirement may 
explain why no significant association was found between 
language and early detection, as the system can efficiently 
translate and analyze data regardless of its language of 
origin.
A few limitations of this study are worth highlight­
ing. First, this study has focused on the performance of 
the EIOS system from a regional perspective. As such, 
early detection, as reported in this study, is based on the 
EIOS system’s ability to capture a signal of an acute pub­
lic health event from open sources before official noti­
fication to WHO. There are several other surveillance 
systems for early event detection within the countries; 
therefore, these results may not necessarily be extrapo­
lated to the system’s performance within each country. 
A study of how the EIOS system has performed within 
each country from a national-level perspective may be 
warranted.
Second, the predictors analyzed in this study are 
not exhaustive enough to explain the performance of 
the EIOS system in detecting events early. Other fac­
tors, such as human moderation and heightened media 
awareness during periods of epidemics and pandem­
ics and the expansion of the EIOS system use over the 
years should be contextually considered when interpret­
ing these findings. Human moderation, which involves 
judgment-based triage of information published on the 
EIOS system by epidemiologists at WHO AFRO, was not 
modelled in our study, potentially leading to an underes­
timation of detection capacity or improved system per­
formance by filtering noise.
Conclusions
Despite these limitations, this study has provided a 
detailed understanding of the EIOS system’s performance 
for the early detection of public health events in the Afri­
can region. The EIOS system’s main strengths lie in its 
ability to pool information from a wide variety of sources 
over the internet, including from expert epidemic intel­
ligence systems.
We recommend that developers of the EIOS system 
consider streaming in more social media sources to 
optimize the performance of the EIOS system for early 
detection of public health events in the African region. 
Additionally, community radios are an important source 
of local news about health events [28, 29]. We recom­
mend incorporating local community radios as additional 
sources on the EIOS system to enrich its feed for public 
health intelligence.

Abstract: Introduction Public health today is challenged by a wide array of hazards that threaten humans, often resulting in high rates of morbidity and mortality when they strike. These events should be detected and responded to as early as possible to save lives and minimize their impact. The Epidemic Intelligence from Open Sources (EIOS) system leverages natural language processing and machine learning techniques for the early detection of public health events from open-source information using an all-hazards approach. In this study, we quantitatively evaluate the performance of the EIOS system for the early detection of outbreaks and health emergencies in the African region. Methods We retrospectively searched the EIOS system to determine if a signal was found on the system for each public health event notified to WHO by the 47 countries in the African region from 2018 to 2023. We computed the proportion of public health event detected by the EIOS system, its sensitivity, harmonic mean, and timeliness. We assessed the association between selected predictors (year of report, hazard type, subregion, source type, and language of source) and early detection of public health events on the EIOS system using a multivariable logistic regression model. Results We found a detection proportion of 81.0% and a sensitivity of 47.4%, with a harmonic mean of 59.8%. The proportion of events detected steadily increased over the years and sensitivity increased from a baseline of 44.1% in 2018 to 47.3% in 2023. Signals for more than 80.0% of the public health events notified to WHO in 28 countries were detected on the EIOS system. In 22 countries, signals of at least 50% of the public health events were detected early, that is, before official notification from the National Authorities to WHO. The median time between detection on the EIOS system and notification to WHO was zero days. We found that the type of hazard (infectious and zoonotic), the subregion (West and Central Africa), and the type of source (medical and social media) were associated with early detection.
